objective.subject: Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026-2028)
objective.title: Simple phenomena of magnetism
objective.syllabus_verbatim: Describe a magnetic field as a region in which a magnetic pole experiences a force.
objective.related_verbatim: Draw the pattern and direction of magnetic field lines around a bar magnet.
objective.supplement_verbatim: Know that the relative strength of a magnetic field is represented by the spacing of the magnetic field lines.
objective.depth_ref: Core objectives 5, 6, 8 with Supplement 11. Full-mark answers draw arrows on every line, run them N to S outside the magnet, and never let two lines cross.

lineage._note: Tier 2. Set by hand. The honest statement comes first and is not buried.
lineage.honest_statement: This topic has no Islamic thread. Magnetism was not shaped in the Muslim world, and we are not going to invent a connection to make the story tidier. Wisdom is taken wherever it is found — so we go to the man who actually did this.
lineage.contribution: Introduced the idea of a field: that the space around a magnet is itself altered, and that this alteration can be drawn as lines. Physics had treated magnetism as attraction across empty space; Faraday made the space the subject.
lineage.how_they_thought: Faraday had almost no mathematics — he had left school at thirteen and was apprenticed to a bookbinder. He could not write the equations, so he refused to work in equations. He thought in pictures: he imagined lines of force filling the space, drew them, and then designed experiments to test whether the picture predicted correctly. It did. Twenty years later Maxwell turned Faraday's pictures into the equations Faraday could never have written — and said openly that the ideas were Faraday's.
lineage.citation: Faraday, Experimental Researches in Electricity (1839–55), Series XXVIII on lines of force
lineage.why_it_matters: A child who thinks they are 'not a maths person' should meet Faraday before they conclude anything about themselves.

algorithm._note: The universal layer. Present regardless of tier.
algorithm.name: Make the invisible visible
steps: You cannot see the force. Stop trying to.
Find something small that the force can move — iron filings, a compass needle.
Put it at one point. Note which way it turns. That is the direction of the field at that point.
Repeat at many points. The pattern that emerges is the field.
Read the spacing: where the lines crowd, the field is strong; where they spread, it is weak.
You now have a picture of something invisible — and a picture you can predict with.
socratic_prompts: You are told there is a force in this space, and you can see nothing at all. What could you put there to find out?
The compass needle turns and stops. What exactly has it told you — how strong the field is, or which way it points?
Here are two field drawings, one crowded and one spread out. Which magnet is stronger, and how do you know without measuring anything?
Could two field lines ever cross? Think about what a compass placed exactly on the crossing point would have to do.

cambridge_form.statement: Describe a magnetic field as a region in which a magnetic pole experiences a force.
method: A field is a region — not a thing. It is where a pole would feel a force.
Field lines run from N to S outside the magnet, and every line carries an arrow.
The direction at a point is the direction of the force on a north pole placed there.
Spacing encodes strength: crowded lines mean a strong field.
Lines never cross — a compass at a crossing point would have to point two ways at once.
cambridge_form.general_result: Field lines: N → S outside the magnet, arrowed, never crossing, closest together at the poles.
cambridge_form.command_words: “Draw the pattern and direction” — the arrows carry marks. A drawing without arrows is an incomplete answer, however neat the curves.

worked.problem: Draw the magnetic field around a single bar magnet.
steps: Lines leave the N pole and return to the S pole.
They bulge outward, symmetrical about the magnet.
They are most crowded at the two poles — that is where the field is strongest.
Arrows on every line, pointing N → S outside the magnet.
No line touches or crosses another.
worked.answer: A symmetrical arrowed pattern, densest at the poles

apply._note: Withhold-then-reveal. The child predicts before the pattern is shown.
apply.problem: Two bar magnets are placed end to end with their N poles facing each other, a small gap apart. Sketch the field in the gap, and mark the point where a compass needle would not know which way to turn.
apply.hint: Both poles are pushing outward. What happens exactly halfway between two equal pushes?
reveal_steps: Each N pole sends its lines outward, so in the gap the two sets of lines are heading straight at each other.
They cannot cross, so they turn aside — the field in the gap bends away to the sides.
Exactly halfway between two equal poles, the two pushes cancel completely.
At that point the field is zero. A compass there has no direction to take — it is called a neutral point.
That is the whole idea in one dot: the field is a real thing at every point in space, and here that thing happens to be nothing.
apply.answer: Field lines bend away sideways; a neutral point sits exactly midway between the two N poles, where the field is zero.
apply.mark_scheme: B1 for lines curving away from the gap. B1 for arrows shown on the lines. B1 for the neutral point marked at the midpoint. Candidates lose the mark if any two lines are drawn crossing.
apply.closing: with a method a bookbinder’s apprentice drew in London, because he could not write the equations

ask._note: Grounded Q&A. Frozen answers, matched deterministically in ask.py. No model, no network.
suggested: Why can't two field lines cross?
How do we know the field is there if we can't see it?
Why did Faraday draw instead of using equations?

qa.answer: A field is a region, not an object. It is the space around a magnet where a magnetic pole would feel a force. Before Faraday, physics said magnets simply attracted across empty space. He said the space itself is changed — and that the change can be drawn.

Because the direction at a point is unique. A field line's direction is where a north pole would be pushed. If two lines crossed, a compass placed exactly there would have to point two different ways at once, which it cannot. So lines bend around each other instead.

You put something in it that the force can move — iron filings or a compass needle. Each one turns to line up with the field at its own point. Do that at many points and the pattern appears. You never see the field; you see what it does, and that is enough to predict with.

Because he could not do the mathematics. Faraday left school at thirteen and was apprenticed to a bookbinder. Rather than fake the algebra, he thought in pictures — lines of force he could draw and then test by experiment. Twenty years later Maxwell turned those pictures into equations, and said openly the ideas were Faraday's.

A point where the field is exactly zero because two equal fields cancel. Put two N poles facing each other and, precisely halfway between, the two pushes are equal and opposite. A compass placed there has no direction to take. It is the clearest proof that a field is a real thing at every point — here that thing happens to be nothing.

Read the spacing. Where the lines crowd together the field is strong; where they spread out it is weak. That is why the lines bunch at the poles — the field is strongest there. Cambridge tests this directly in objective 4.1.11.

story.title: The field
the_word: A field is not an object. It is a region — every point in the space around a magnet where a pole would feel a force.
Before Faraday, physics said magnets simply pulled on each other across empty space. Nobody asked what the space in between was doing, because the answer was assumed to be: nothing.
Faraday's move was to make the empty space the subject. He said it is not empty — it is altered, at every point, and the alteration can be drawn.
That idea outgrew magnetism entirely. Electric fields, gravitational fields, the quantum fields modern physics is built on — all of them are Faraday's picture, extended.

why.lead: He arrived at it because he could not do the mathematics:
why.after: Faraday left school at thirteen and was apprenticed to a bookbinder. He had no algebra to speak of and never pretended otherwise. So instead of deriving, he drew — lines of force filling space — and then designed experiments to test whether the drawing predicted correctly. It did, again and again. Twenty years later Maxwell turned those drawings into the equations Faraday could never have written, and said openly that the ideas were Faraday's.

where_now: A current in a field feels a force. That is a motor — and it is the direct descendant of Faraday's picture.
Move a magnet near a coil and you generate current. Faraday found this too. Almost all the world's electricity is made this way.
MRI puts your body in an enormous field and reads what the atoms do. The scan is a field map.
Electric, gravitational, quantum. The word and the picture are Faraday's, borrowed by physics and never given back.

keywords._note: IGCSE is marked on precise terminology and on obeying the command word. Both are listed.
command_words: State what happens or what something looks like. No reasons required — but no marks for reasons either, so do not waste time.
Give the reason why. A description alone scores nothing here.
One line. No working, no justification.
A labelled diagram. For fields, arrows are worth marks — a drawing without them is incomplete however neat.
Recall it. Usually one mark, usually a definition.
terms: A region in which a magnetic pole experiences a force. Say region — not 'area around a magnet'.
A line showing the direction of the force on a north pole placed at that point.
The direction of the force on a north pole. Always specify north.
A magnetic material becoming a magnet when placed in a magnetic field.
Made of steel; keeps its magnetism.
Made of soft iron; loses its magnetism easily.
A point where two fields cancel and the resultant field is zero.
A material that can be attracted by a magnet and can be magnetised — iron, steel, cobalt, nickel.

practice.intro: Draw each one before you reveal it. Arrows count.

items.q: Draw the field pattern around a single bar magnet.
items.form: Lines N → S outside the magnet, symmetrical, arrowed
items.ans: Most crowded at the poles — that is where the field is strongest.

items.q: State the direction of a magnetic field at a point.
items.form: The direction of the force on a north pole at that point

items.q: Explain why two field lines can never cross.
items.form: The direction at a point is unique
items.ans: A compass at the crossing point would have to point two ways at once, which is impossible.

items.q: Two field diagrams: one with crowded lines, one with spread lines. Which magnet is stronger?
Describe how to plot a magnetic field using a compass.
items.ans: Place the compass, mark the needle direction, move it to the mark, repeat; join the marks into a line.

items.q: State the difference between a permanent and a temporary magnet.
items.ans: Steel keeps its magnetism (permanent); soft iron loses it easily (temporary).

items.q: Two N poles face each other. Sketch the field and mark where it is zero.
items.form: Lines curve away; neutral point at the midpoint
items.ans: Equal and opposite fields cancel exactly midway.

items.q: Explain what is meant by induced magnetism.
items.form: A magnetic material becomes a magnet in a field
items.ans: It is magnetised by being placed in a magnetic field, without contact being needed.

framing.heading: Why this was hard
body: The accepted explanation was action at a distance — which names the mystery rather than explaining it. The space between two magnets was assumed to be doing nothing at all.
Faraday could not join that argument on its own terms, because he had almost no mathematics. So he asked a physical question instead: what is the space in between actually doing?

The limitation is what forced the new idea. Had he been able to derive, he would probably have derived — and the field, the single most important concept in modern physics, might have waited another generation.
